def: The middle household income for an area, published by HUD and adjusted for household size. Tax credit income limits are set as a percentage of it, usually 50% or 60%.
The share of a building that's affordable, measured by units or floor space, whichever is lower. Multiplied by eligible basis to get qualified basis.
The annual credit rate: at least 9% for new construction and rehab in competitive deals, and at least 4% for bond-financed deals and building acquisitions.
Counting 130% of eligible basis for a building in a QCT, a DDA or one the state designates, which raises the credit amount.
All the sources of money that pay for a deal, layered from the first mortgage down to equity.
The first 15 years of a tax credit property's life, when the IRS can recapture credits if the rules are broken.
A federal law that encourages banks to invest in the communities they serve. Tax credit investments can count, which is why banks are big buyers.
An area HUD designates where land, construction and utility costs are high relative to incomes. Deals there can get the 30% basis boost.
The part of the developer fee left in the deal as a source of funds and paid later from cash flow.
Net operating income divided by the annual mortgage payment. Lenders require a minimum, often 1.15 to 1.25, which limits how big the loan can be.
The costs of a building that can earn credits: mostly construction and related soft costs, not land.
The cash investors pay into a deal in exchange for its tax credits and tax losses.
At least 15 more years of affordability after the compliance period, enforced by the state through a recorded agreement.
The IRS form the state issues for each building once it's placed in service, confirming its credit amount. The owner needs it to claim credits.
The form a state agency files with the IRS to report a property's noncompliance.
The owner that runs the deal, usually a developer affiliate, holding a tiny ownership share.
Rent plus a utility allowance for tenant-paid utilities. The tax credit cap applies to gross rent.
A HUD block grant program that states and cities use for affordable housing loans and grants.
Rental assistance that helps a household pay rent at a private apartment. The renter usually pays about 30% of income.
A set-aside option where unit income limits range from 20% to 80% of AMI but must average 60% or less.
The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, Section 42 of the tax code. The main federal tool for building affordable rental housing.
The investor in a tax credit partnership, usually owning 99% or more to receive the credits.
Land use restriction agreement: the recorded document that keeps a property affordable for its full term, whoever owns it.
A third-party report, required before an award, showing there's demand for the apartments at the proposed rents.
The share of units a deal must keep affordable: 20/50, 40/60 or income averaging.
The income limits HUD publishes each year for tax credit and bond-financed properties.
Rental income minus vacancy and operating costs, before the mortgage payment.
When a building is ready for residents. Generally starts the credit and compliance clocks (the owner can choose to start them the next year).
Tax-exempt bonds issued for private projects like affordable housing. Using enough of them unlocks 4% credits.
Each state's rulebook and scoring system for awarding tax credits.
A lower-income census tract designated by HUD. Deals there can get the 30% basis boost.
Eligible basis times the applicable fraction. Multiplied by the credit rate to get the annual credit.
A process that can let an owner end the affordability period after year 14 if the state can't find a buyer at a formula price. Many states require owners to waive it.
The Rental Assistance Demonstration: converts public housing to long-term Section 8 contracts so it can be financed and rebuilt.
The IRS taking back part of the credits already claimed, with interest, if a building's qualified basis drops during the compliance period.
A right for a nonprofit, tenant group or agency to buy a property after year 15 at a minimum price.
Below-market or forgivable loans and grants that fill financing gaps.
A firm that pools investor money into funds and invests it in tax credit deals.
An estimate of tenant-paid utility costs, subtracted from the gross rent cap to get the maximum rent.
Each state's annual limit on private activity bonds. 4% deals compete for it.
The end of the compliance period, when investors usually exit and ownership often changes hands.
